content.text: {"relation": "NOVEL", "consensus_summary": "All four blind responses converge on a symbolic-theological identification: the Sabbath day signifies sacred rest — God's creation rest, functioning as a covenant sign for Israel and a memorial of redemption, and read typologically (via Hebrews 3-4 and Colossians 2:16-17) as the spiritual rest believers enter in Christ and the eschatological rest of the world to come. Alternatives concern practice (Sunday transfer, seventh-day obligation, abolition) and secondary symbolisms (millennial week, liberation/justice, sanctified time).", "book_summary": "The book gives a lexical-grammatical identification, not a symbolic one: 'the day of the sabbath' is the marked member of the sabbath-unit — the specific day within the unit, parallel to 'the day of the new moon' within the month (Ezekiel 46:1 juxtaposing the two genitives). When Scripture means the resting member itself it doubles the word (shabbat shabbaton, 'sabbath of rest'), wherever that rest falls — seventh day, Day of Atonement, or the land's seventh year — and Greek mirrors the construction (hē hēmera tōn sabbatōn).", "consensus_core_identification": "The Sabbath day symbolizes divine rest: creation rest, covenant sign, and typological/eschatological rest fulfilled in Christ.", "book_core_identification": "'Yom ha-shabbat' is a grammatical construction designating the marked day-member of the sabbath-unit (analogous to the day of the new moon within the month), distinguished from the doubled form shabbat shabbaton which denotes the resting observance itself in any of its calendrical instantiations.", "core_relation": "NO_CONSENSUS", "extension_relation": "NO_BASELINE", "boundary_disagreement": "There is no direct boundary dispute over shared cases; however, the book implicitly reclassifies the phrase's referent from a theological symbol of rest to a structural term within a temporal-unit system, and extends the shabbat-shabbaton category beyond the weekly seventh day to the Day of Atonement and the sabbatical year — a taxonomic move none of the consensus responses makes.", "material_contradiction": "None. The book's linguistic analysis of how 'day of the sabbath' functions grammatically does not deny that the Sabbath signifies rest in Christ or covenant identity; it simply answers a different question and never engages the typological reading.", "rationale": "The blind consensus operates entirely on the plane of theological symbolism (rest, covenant sign, christological fulfillment, eschatology). The book's entry operates on the plane of lexical semantics and construct-grammar: what the genitive phrase 'yom ha-shabbat' marks within a unit-system, and how it differs from shabbat shabbaton. No consensus response or listed alternative anticipates this identification, and the book neither affirms nor rejects the symbolic consensus. Since novelty is defined as absence from consensus rather than contradiction, NOVEL is the correct verdict; DIVERGENT would require the book to replace or negate the consensus referent, which it does not do.", "citation_support": "PARTIAL", "strongest_objection": "One could argue the book's entry is merely definitional groundwork compatible with (and presupposed by) the consensus, so the relation should be MATCH at the trivial level that both agree the phrase names the sacred seventh day; also, the printed citations do support the grammatical claims (Ezek 46:1 pairs sabbath and new-moon day; Ex 31:15 and Lev 23:32 show shabbat shabbaton for the seventh day and Atonement), so calling the identification 'novel' may overstate a difference that is really one of genre — glossary lexicography versus symbolic theology.", "confidence": "medium"}
